transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-12 16:00 UTC | Duration 75m | Recorded by Fireflies
Attendees: Jordan Li (Redwood AE), Marisol Gomez (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (Redwood Infra), Nina Roberts (BrightLabs Head of ML), Owen Lee (BrightLabs SRE), Priyanka Rao (BrightLabs ML infra), Marcus Chen (BrightLabs CTO)

[00:00:00] Jordan: all right everyone thanks for joining, I know we have a packed agenda, we'll focus on the on-prem perf followup and the hybrid MoE routing questions. quick intros — marisol from the se side and ethan on infra.
[00:00:18] Marisol: hi all, quick note: we'll jump between model tuning and infra shape. forgive my typing, i'll drop config links after.
[00:00:33] Nina: thanks, priority for us is hitting <100ms p95 for our realtime assistant at 2k context for ~60 reqs/s, while keeping costs down, and avoiding hallucination regressions after quant.
[00:00:48] Owen: also network headroom is tight in our rack, want to understand NVLink vs ethernet costs for KV cache heavy workloads.
[00:01:05] Marisol: understood. first item: MoE routing cost. you mentioned in the doc that ~30% of tokens route to multiple experts causing cross-GPU exchange spikes? can you confirm patterns?
[00:01:22] Priyanka: yeah our telemetry shows a token affinity pattern where about 18% of tokens hit cold expert sets during long dialogues which trips halo exchange. sometimes the router picks 3 experts not 2 for some tokens, and that increases PCIe transfers.
[00:01:40] Ethan: can you share the histogram, priya? the difference between 2->3 experts is brutal for latency.
[00:01:48] Nina: i'll share the telemetry after, but basically we see routing churn when users switch contexts mid-session.
[00:02:02] Marisol: two levers: one, tighten gating threshold so fewer tokens go to additional experts (reduce compute but risk quality drop). two, implement token-affinity sticky routing to prefer experts with hot KV caches — reduces data movement but complicates load balancing.
[00:02:25] Marcus: sticky routing sounds good if it avoids cross-GPU KV cache misses. what's the downside?
[00:02:33] Marisol: potential skew: you can create hot expert nodes that saturate a GPU, so need a background rebalance + slow-roll migration. also for long tail tokens we may need fallback to dense path.
[00:02:48] Jordan: quick interjection — we have a rollout pattern that keeps a fallback dense model on standby; if routing latency or error rates degrade we transparently fall back.
[00:02:59] Owen: okay good. next: RoPE scaling — our evals show perplexity increases beyond 1k tokens for Qwen-style rotary offsets when we quantize. any thoughts?
[00:03:16] Marisol: RoPE (rotary positional enc) numerics are sensitive when you quantize weights and activations, especially with 4-bit schemes. two common mitigations: scale the RoPE frequency (linear rescale) for longer contexts and use mixed-precision for the RoPE projection layers.
[00:03:35] Priyanka: mixed-precision for just the RoPE projections — is that supported in your runtime?
[00:03:40] Ethan: yes we can selectively keep some layers at fp16 while others are awq/4-bit. runtime supports per-layer dtype annotations and kernel selection. there's a perf hit but it's often negligible compared to quality regained.
[00:03:57] Nina: what's the rough token cost delta for keeping RoPE in fp16?
[00:04:02] Ethan: small — maybe 3-5% extra memory bandwidth, negligible extra GPU cycles vs full fp16.
[00:04:12] Marisol: another nuance: for Mistral and Llama families the RoPE embedding magnitude differs; Qwen uses a slightly different base frequency making the scaling factor non-uniform. we recommend per-model calibration sheets — marisol to share.
[00:04:31] Jordan: noted. on KV cache: priya you said eviction thrash — can you describe cache key cardinality?
[00:04:40] Priyanka: we have about 120k unique prefixes for hot sessions, but effective hot set is ~8k. eviction policy sometimes kicks entries out because batch interleaving from other users clears them. we tried LRU but the pattern suffers.
[00:04:58] Marisol: two suggestions: prefix-aware caching and per-tenant sticky partitions. prefix-aware means don't evict entries that are likely to be reused within X tokens; we heuristically compute reuse probability from prompt hist. sticky partitions means route a tenant's sessions to the same expert/partition to increase local hit rate.
[00:05:17] Marcus: sticky partitions again raises skew concerns. what about sharding the KV cache by prefix hash to avoid hotspots?
[00:05:25] Ethan: sharding can help but increases cross-GPU fetchs when a single session's prefixes hash to many shards. Better is tenant-locality + small bloom filter to test local presence before remote fetch.
[00:05:39] Nina: are there built-in Redwood tools for tracing KV cache misses? we only have coarse metrics.
[00:05:45] Jordan: yes, we can provide detailed KV cache traces showing hit/miss per step and per-token latency. Marisol will annotate with likely root causes.
[00:05:55] Marisol: i'll add heuristics to the traces so you can filter by prefix length and tenant id.
[00:06:02] Owen: moving to batching: our tail latency comes from naive batching at the grpc layer, we batch aggressively to save tokens but p95 spikes. any recommended policy?
[00:06:15] Marisol: two axes: batch size and batch deadline. aggressive batching (big size) reduces compute cost but increases latency. use dynamic batching with workload-aware deadlines: e.g. prefer sub-ms deadlines for interactive routes, and adapt deadline based on recent latency feedback to hit p95 target. also use continuous batching for decoder workloads to reduce kernel launch overhead.
[00:06:37] Priyanka: continuous batching — is that the KV cache aware flow?
[00:06:41] Ethan: yes continuous batching keeps the runtime ready to append tokens into the same execution stream as long as deps are satisfied — plays very well with prefix caching. it reduces schedule jitter.
[00:06:54] Nina: does Redwood runtime support preemptible priority lanes? we want critical user flows to jump the queue.
[00:06:59] Jordan: yes, priority lanes configurable via route policy. you can reserve a fraction of slots for low-latency, charge premium or limited token caps.
[00:07:10] Marisol: for on-prem, note that priority lane isolation still consumes NVLink/PCIe bandwidth — if the hardware is saturated you still see tail. need to provision network headroom.
[00:07:22] Owen: on the network subject: our Mellanox cards claim 200Gbps but we see link saturation during large KV misses. are we seeing serialization from PCIe as well?
[00:07:35] Ethan: yes, PCIe root complex and CPU memory copy overhead matters. crossing CPU for remote fetches introduces latency; best case is NVLink / GPU Direct RDMA path. do you have NVLink fully enabled between GPUs in your nodes or are you using mixed nodes across NIC boundaries?
[00:07:54] Priyanka: mixed nodes. some racks are older without NVLink across all GPUs.
[00:07:58] Ethan: that's the culprit. when you don't have full NVLink, expert exchange hits NIC and PCIe stacks and you pay big latency and jitter. recommendation: collocate experts such that frequent expert pairs live on the same NVLink domain, or fall back to dense routing for those hot pairs.
[00:08:18] Marisol: we can run an affinity partitioning algorithm that clusters experts by co-access frequency and reassigns them to GPUs to minimize cross-node traffic. we'll provide the script.
[00:08:26] Marcus: what about quantization — we saw 4-bit AWQ reduced memory by ~2.4x but some tail-case hallucinations increased. any reproducible mitigations?
[00:08:38] Marisol: AWQ/LSQ schemes differ; common approaches: 1) per-channel quant for attention and MLP projections, 2) keep layernorm/softmax in fp16, 3) use calibration with representative prompt set and monitor a small eval with targeted RAG prompts to detect hallucination regressions. also temperature and sampling tweaks sometimes mask regressions but that's risky.
[00:08:59] Nina: do you have automated eval harness we can run on our prompts?
[00:09:03] Jordan: yes we'll share the Redwood eval harness; you can plug in your prompt corpus — it'll run reference metrics including exact match, factuality heuristics, and token-level divergence.
[00:09:14] Owen: in terms of throughput, what quant config gives best cost/latency sweet spot?
[00:09:20] Ethan: typically awq 4-bit with per-channel on query/key/project + keep softmax fp16 gives ~2.2-2.6x speedup on memory-bound inference and minimal quality impact on short context <512. For longer context you see more numeric drift, so mixed-precision RoPE and some MLPs kept at fp16 is recommended.
[00:09:40] Marisol: also consider dynamic quant fallback: route high-importance requests (identified by route metadata) to fp16 path and everything else to quant path. That reduces unit cost but preserves quality for SLAs.
[00:09:51] Priyanka: ok but we want an automated detector for when to fallback mid-session — e.g., if perplexity jumps or token entropy changes.
[00:09:59] Marisol: runtime can expose token-level confidence heuristics; we can trigger a fallback at next token boundary. it's not free — you pay for a switch and KV warming — but it's feasible.
[00:10:12] Nina: back to MoE routing cost: you mentioned gating thresholds — what are concrete numbers to try?
[00:10:18] Marisol: start with raising the gating bias so that average experts per token moves from 2.0 to 1.6. monitor accuracy on eval set. Another knob is top-k gating instead of soft-gating which tends to limit to fixed expert count (deterministic).
[00:10:33] Ethan: top-k gating reduces variance at cost of possibly worse distribution balance. combine with load-shedding: if a GPU is seeing >85% util per step, route some tokens to dense fallback.
[00:10:45] Marcus: curious about cost math — what's the incremental token cost when moving from 2->2.5 experts avg?
[00:10:51] Marisol: roughly linear: 2->2.5 typically ~25% extra compute and 30-40% extra cross-GPU traffic depending on expert placement. that's why affinity and sticky routing saves real dollars.
[00:11:05] Nina: ok good to know. now, we ran a short bench of Llama-2-70B vs Mistral-34B with same prompt set — Mistral was cheaper but had more context drift beyond 1.5k. what's the tradeoff?
[00:11:19] Marisol: architecture: Mistral-style models optimize dense compute and attention patterns for throughput but tend to use different positional embeddings, so RoPE behavior differs. Llama-2's 70b might be slower but may sustain longer context with quant applied. Qwen also has different attention scaling. Best practice: per-model quant + RoPE config, don't apply a one-size-fits-all.
[00:11:39] Priyanka: can Redwood runtime maintain multiple model variants and route by cost? e.g., default to quant Mistral, fallback to dense Llama for long context?
[00:11:47] Jordan: yes, smart routing policy can route by context length and cost tier. you'll get a transparent policy layer and metrics on how often fallback triggers.
[00:11:57] Owen: any notes on on-prem security and KMS integration when running mixed precision? nothing specific but curious if quant artifacts leak anything extra.
[00:12:06] Marisol: quantization does not change the encryption surface — model weights are still protected at rest. for on-prem, you control KMS/HSM. we store only metadata with the control plane if using Redwood Private; in fully air-gapped setups the control plane runs as a local process.
[00:12:20] Marcus: next, scheduling for pilot — what's minimal hardware to replicate our perf?
[00:12:25] Ethan: for your target (2k ctx, 2k context p95 <100ms at 60 reqs/s) I'd recommend 8x A100 80GB with full NVLink per node or 4x H100 with NVLink depending on model; MoE benefits from more GPUs to distribute experts but only if NVLink mesh exists. For small pilot 4x A100 with careful expert placement + sticky routing might be enough to validate.
[00:12:47] Nina: cost estimates?
[00:12:50] Jordan: we'll send an estimated infra bill and Redwood Dedicated pricing options in the followup.
[00:12:56] Marisol: last technical note: rope scaling numeric trick — use a hybrid positional table where you linearly rescale angles beyond a threshold and apply small damping for high frequencies to reduce oscillation after quant. we can push a sample patch.
[00:13:12] Priyanka: appreciate that. can you also share recommended perf counters to capture (e.g., PCIe bytes, NVLink:ts, kernel launch lat, kv-cache hit rate per step)?
[00:13:22] Ethan: yes: per-step kernel time, NVLink bytes per step, PCIe transfers, CPU->GPU memcpy time, KV cache hit ratio, router expert distribution histogram, average experts/token, and batch queue wait time. we'll share a prom-exporter list.
[00:13:36] Nina: great. shall we recap next steps?
[00:13:40] Jordan: recap: get per-token traces from BrightLabs (Priyanka/Nina) plus NVLink topology and rack layout (Owen). Redwood to share affinity partition script, eval harness, quant profiles and suggested batching policy. pilot kickoff target 2026-03-24.
[00:13:58] Marcus: agreed.
[00:14:02] Marisol: one quick question — if we do sticky tenant routing, how do we avoid long-term skew we discussed? what's safe rebalance cadence?
[00:14:11] Ethan: conservative rebalance every 12-24 hours with rolling migration windows is safe for production; for pilot you can rebalance weekly. also apply rate-limited weight moves.
[00:14:24] Nina: ok thanks everyone. we'll collect the telemetry and prioritize the experiments.
[00:14:30] Jordan: thanks team, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[00:14:34] -- end of recorded transcript excerpt --

Notes about transcription: occasional words may be mistranscribed (e.g., "awq" as "awk"), speaker overlaps noted. Full raw audio stored in CRM link. Links shared in chat: /links/redwood/affinity-script, /links/redwood/eval-harness, /links/redwood/quant-profiles

Additional context (not part of recording): Redwood recommends running the affinity clustering with a sample of ~1M tokens of cross-session traces to stabilize expert placement. Also suggested microbench commands: redwood-bench --model <variant> --ctx 2048 --batch 1..8 --measure nvlink,pci.
